Naive rationalism not only failed to answer this question. It barely even asked it.
Why, then, did human beings abandon the position we are calling naive rationalism?
Why did they reject a viewpoint that initially seemed completely natural to them and that they had first accepted without qualification, even if unconsciously and without justification?

On the basis of psychological and historical experience, we can say with a high degree of confidence that they did not abandon it because their discourse repeatedly failed to match objective reality or experience.
First, the “theories” produced by myth-makers usually could not be tested experimentally in any meaningful way.
Second, the fact that belief in magical predictions survives quite happily even in our own time shows that being disproved by experience has only a very limited effect on people.
Finally, myth-makers demanded so little from their “theories” that it was usually easy enough to modify them so that they could somehow “explain” almost any fact of experience.
We can therefore reasonably say that naive rationalism was not destroyed by comparing mythical “theories” with purified facts—that is, with reality.
Its collapse came instead from a purely internal source.
Naive faith in reason and discourse was destroyed by the simple fact that there were many myth-makers, and they did not all say the same thing.
What seemed completely convincing to one person did not convince another at all, and vice versa.

One person might insist that the “truth” was that “in the beginning there was the Serpent, which…” while another insisted on an entirely different “truth”: “in the beginning” there was not the Serpent but “the Sun, which…”
Yet neither myth-maker could defend their “truth” with anything more than the coherence of their discourse—and all the myths possessed this coherence.
So neither party could convince the other in a dispute or bring the other over to their side. In fact, any genuine dispute was impossible.
We are simply left with the hard fact that there are mutually contradictory statements.
If we rely only on rational—that is, discursive or logical—criteria, then it is strictly impossible to choose between them.
This conflict, discovered within reason itself, or within discourse itself, forced human beings to abandon the construction of naive rationalism.
Once confronted, for example, with many mutually contradictory myths, they could no longer maintain that every coherent discourse was true.
In collapsing, naive rationalism gave rise to scepticism, a doctrine diametrically opposed to it but just as “naive” and just as rationalistic.
Primitive rationalism had naively assumed that every coherent discourse—every myth—was true.

Once this same rationalism became sceptical, it began to maintain just as naively that every discourse or myth was false or doubtful, that none could satisfy reason, and that any one of them could be replaced by any other.
“In the beginning there was the Serpent.” Why not?
But it could just as well have been the Sun—or anything else one happens to choose.
This naive scepticism is just as rationalistic as naive rationalism.
In both cases, it is silently assumed that reason or discourse is the only means by which truth can be reached.
The only difference is that rationalism assumes that reason always reaches the truth, whereas scepticism assumes that it never does.
Of course, the appearance of this “first” scepticism already represents a certain advance, because reason can, in fact, be wrong.
But scepticism itself becomes mistaken when it assumes that reason is always wrong.
Or, more precisely, it is not mistaken in saying that reason will never reach truth by itself. What it gets wrong is the conclusion that truth is therefore inaccessible to human beings.
At this stage, scepticism has not yet understood that human beings reach truth not through reason alone, but also, for example, through experience.
In any case, human beings could hardly remain satisfied with this sceptical “solution.”
As long as human beings speak, they will continue trying to say true things that satisfy them fully and finally.

And since we have a “natural” tendency toward rationalism, and since the logical possibilities of rationalism are not exhausted by its naive or dogmatic form, the reaction against naive rationalist scepticism was itself rationalistic.
We can say that naive rational scepticism transformed naive or dogmatic rationalism into critical rationalism.
Rationalism could no longer claim that reason always and automatically produces coherent discourses that reach the truth.
Instead, it began to argue that reason reaches truth only after critically reworking the discourses it produces.
But this reworking is itself carried out through purely rational—that is, discursive—means. So the basic principle of rationalism remains unchanged.
In the end, this critical reworking of discourse amounts to identification.
Rationalism had become sceptical after discovering that one and the same capacity for discourse—one and the same reason—could assert different and incompatible things with equal force.
For example, reason could say that “in the beginning” there was the Serpent, or it could say that “in the beginning” there was the Sun.
But if we identify the Serpent with the Sun, the difficulty disappears and rational truth is saved.
Critical rationalism therefore preserves truth by claiming that the contradiction lies not in the meaning but merely in the words:
“Serpent” and “Sun” are two different words for the same thing, two words carrying one and the same meaning.
In principle, this way of solving the problem is completely satisfactory.
If all possible discourses really do have one and the same meaning, then there is no reason not to regard all of them as identical.
Strictly speaking, if this were genuinely the case, every meaningful discourse would explain everything and would therefore be absolutely true—that is, it would satisfy reason permanently.
There is nothing especially strange about this.
Even today we constantly use critical identifications of this kind.
For example, from our present point of view, it is equally convincing to say that “snow is made of water” and that “snow is made of oxygen and hydrogen.”

Yet at “first” sight—that is, from an uncritical or naive point of view—the words and meanings “water” and “hydrogen and oxygen” seem to have about as much, or as little, in common as “Serpent” and “Sun.”
Critical analysis, however, shows that they refer to the same thing.

We therefore have no reason to say sceptically that we do not know what snow is made of. Once the two claims have been critically identified, both can be preserved even though they initially seemed to exclude one another.

It is easy to show that, in its rational structure, contemporary science consists largely of identifications of this kind. These are based above all on distinguishing, within words, between their phonetic form and their semantic content.
By making critical identifications, reason really can eliminate a very large number of contradictions.
But as long as it fails to eliminate all contradictions, it has no convincing answer to scepticism—and never has had one.

It is therefore hardly surprising that, in trying to save this rationalist conception that human beings value so highly, thought eventually followed the path of critical identification all the way to the end.
He had the courage to declare explicitly that all coherent discourses really have one and the same meaning.
He did not deny that we encounter a great variety of statements or discourses. But in his view, this variety was purely phonetic, not semantic.
There can be only one meaning, and this one meaning is nothing other than absolute truth itself.
In one sense, the Parmenidean solution satisfies reason.
Coherence is complete. Contradictions disappear without a trace. Reason can no longer change, reject, or extend the discourse it has produced.
In short, reason becomes certain that it has found absolute truth.
Unfortunately, this particular “truth” reduces itself to one single word, even if that word can of course be pronounced or written in a thousand different ways.
If there is only one meaning, then one word is more than enough.
The existence of additional words expressing that one meaning becomes, from the standpoint of reason, just as contingent and artificial as the existence of different human languages.
For this reason, the Parmenidean solution cannot fully satisfy reason.
It certainly guarantees total coherence and, if one likes, convincingness or truth.
But it achieves this at the cost of communicability—indeed, ultimately at the cost of articulation itself, since in principle only one word is required.
The single Parmenidean word is completely incomprehensible or incommunicable because, once we have said it, we can say absolutely nothing about what it means.
In other words, it is meaningless in the strict sense: it has no meaning that can itself be expressed through a discourse.
The Parmenidean solution therefore rules out discursive communication—that is, conversation.
And reason cannot be satisfied by this.
Every rational, speaking human being who seeks to state the truth also wants to say something about it.

We can therefore say that humanity did not settle for the Parmenidean solution precisely because that solution made discursive communication impossible. It left whoever possessed the truth with only two options: complete silence, or the insane repetition of the same meaningless word over and over again.
Parmenidean rationalism therefore leads inevitably to a new form of scepticism.
Parmenides made an enormous discovery, even if he did not intend to.
He showed that reason, when left entirely to itself, destroys itself.

Reason first began by producing mutually incompatible discourses. It then tried to eliminate the incompatibilities by identifying their contents. And finally it destroyed the very possibility of discourse itself—which means that it destroyed itself.
From this we can draw a conclusion that is, if you like, “sceptical”:
reason is a form of identity with no content of its own.
Whatever content it has must come to it from outside.
By trying to eliminate every contradiction from discourse, reason in practice tends to eliminate every difference and every form of diversity.
That means there is no difference or diversity within reason itself.
All differences must therefore come from something extra-rational or non-rational—something essentially different from discourse (logos).
They come, in other words, from what is usually called actual reality, real being, or simply the real.
Reason does nothing more than name the many-sided reality that exists independently of it.
The diversity of names it produces—words and concepts—is therefore determined by the real diversity that exists independently of reason.
All reason itself can do is discover identities within this real diversity. It can then identify the corresponding words or concepts that refer to the realities it has identified.
This new scepticism is sceptical only about reason.

It claims that reason left to itself cannot satisfy itself—that is, cannot find truth—for the simple reason that it cannot actually say anything. It has no diversity of its own and therefore no content of its own.
But although this “scepticism” finally destroys rationalism, it does not destroy the very concept of truth.
Instead, truth is now defined differently.
A discourse will be called true when its meaning corresponds to the reality that “reveals” itself to human beings.
In other words, this “scepticism” is really nothing other than empiricism.
Empiricism holds that there can be no truth unless discourse is related to reality.
Simply because discourse itself, having no content of its own, would be impossible without reality.

Before rationalism gives way completely and transforms itself into empiricism, however, it makes one final attempt to save its “immanent” conception of truth: the idea that truth is a discourse produced by reason alone that fully satisfies reason.
Naive rationalism had ended in the first scepticism because it regarded all coherent discourses as true even though they contradicted one another.
